description:
Avengers had Doomsday. We have MOONSDAY! But instead of saving the universe, we're keeping the humans exploring it alive and healthy. 🚀

Houston, we have a health problem! And we're not waiting for an emergency transmission to solve it.

We're MOONSDAY, a team bringing AI, technology, and creativity together to monitor astronaut health and make space exploration safer.

Because exploring the Moon and universeis cool, but coming back healthy is cooler. 🌕
summary:
DR. MOON is a spaceflight wellness project designed to explain astronaut health and mission challenges. It brings research, crew self-reports, learning, and motivation into a mission-control interface, while making the limits of its data clear.
The website includes a mission dashboard, interactive astronaut body map, telemetry charts, NASA and CSA educational resources, spaceflight hazards, analytics, settings, training checklists, and a rewards store. The prototype hardware is not working, so vital and habitat readings are fixed fictional examples, labeled as simulated—not real astronaut or NASA data. NASA sources guide context, but do not provide the fictional sample readings. Users can report mood, stress, sleep, symptoms, and activity. Each check-in generates a non-diagnostic summary from the user’s answers; reports remain separate from telemetry.
Users can log workouts, mission tasks, and learning activities to earn points and spend them on humorous digital badges. The integrated local Ollama AI works online or offline and answers educational questions about human health in spaceflight.
Future work includes repairing and connecting the MAX30102 and DHT22, validating real sensor readings, and replacing fictional examples only when trustworthy data is available. DR. MOON is educational, not a medical device or diagnostic system.
details:
DR. MOON is a spaceflight wellness and education platform that helps people explore astronaut health, mission routines, and the challenges of living in space. Its mission-control-style interface brings together educational research, crew self-reports, an AI assistant, training activities, and rewards.

What it does and how it works

The dashboard and interactive astronaut body map present health-related information, while the telemetry pages demonstrate how sensor readings could be displayed. Since our prototype hardware is not currently working, these readings are fixed fictional examples, clearly labeled as simulated—not real astronaut measurements or NASA data. NASA and Canadian Space Agency materials inform the educational context, not the sample values.

Users can voluntarily report their mood, stress, sleep, symptoms, and activity. After submission, the site displays a non-diagnostic summary based only on the user’s own answers. Check-in responses remain separate from the simulated telemetry. Users can also complete learning checklists or log workouts and mission tasks to earn local points, then spend those points on humorous digital badges. The integrated Ollama AI assistant answers educational questions about human health in spaceflight and is designed to work with the project’s online or offline setup.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes spaceflight health topics more approachable and interactive. It demonstrates how educational content, self-reported wellbeing, AI, and gamification can support engagement while making data limitations visible. Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about astronaut health and responsible technology—not to diagnose, treat, or replace professional medical support.

Tools and technology

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules for the website, with a Node.js backend for the application’s local services and Ollama for the AI assistant. The planned hardware includes a MAX30102 optical pulse/oxygen-saturation sensor and a DHT22 ambient temperature/humidity sensor. These sensors are not currently providing working data; repairing and validating the hardware integration is future work.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines a cinematic space-console interface with an interactive astronaut illustration, NASA- and CSA-informed learning, conversational AI, self-check-ins, and playful rewards. We considered privacy, offline use, clear source labels, the difference between user reports and sensor readings, and the risk of presenting simulated data as real. For that reason, demo values are explicitly labeled, check-ins are described as self-reported, and the wellness summary is not presented as a medical diagnosis.
